newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Hijacker captured, hostages freed in south Russia.
newsitem.headline: Hijacker captured, hostages freed in south Russia.

text.p: Police on Monday seized an armed hijacker who had held about 30 hostages in the southern Russian region of Dagestan for almost four hours, a spokesman for the local interior ministry said.

The spokesman said nobody had been hurt in the incident, which came to an end at about 4.45 p.m. (1245 GMT). The gunman was captured alive, after having earlier released all his hostages in stages, the official said.

The unidentified man had earlier boarded the bus heading for the town of Kizlyar armed with an assault rifle and a hand grenade. He then seized the hostages and forced the driver to turn around and stop about 10 km (seven miles) outside Dagestan's capital, Makhachkala, officials said.
The hijacker had demanded a helicopter, police officials said, but they could not confirm an Itar-Tass news agency report than the man had also sought $100,000 in ransom.

As talks with local officials got underway, the hijacker first released two women and four children, another police spokeswoman said. He later freed the other hostages before a police official disarmed him, Tass reported.

Hijackings are not uncommon in Russia's turbulent North Caucasus. Many have involved Chechens fighting for independence for their mainly Moslem region but others have been staged for ransom or unplanned responses to police searches.

Last September, a man armed with a grenade hijacked a bus in Makhachkala, on the Caspian Sea, and demanded a helicopter. He fled by car after freeing the passengers and taking a local politician along as security, and was later reported to have crossed into Chechnya on foot.
There were two bloody hostage-takings just beyond Chechnya's borders during the conflict there from December 1994 to August 1996, one of them at Kizlyar in January 1996.

In 1994, Chechen bandits mounted a series of bus hijackings for ransom across the North Caucausus. They were cited by the Russian authorities as a reason for launching their military campaign against the secessionist rebel government in Chechnya.
But officials in Dagestan, which borders Chechnya, and at the Russian Emergencies Ministry in Moscow said they had no information on who the latest hijacker was or what he wanted.
Tass said that the hijacker was an ethnic Abkhazian, but there was no independent confirmation that he came from Abkazia, a breakaway region of Georgia.
